Name: defense_secrets
Title: Defense Secrets: Arms of Deceit
Experiment: Setting: Japan’s Ministry of Defense is holding an emergency closed-door session about a controversial export deal for next-generation weapons. Unknown to most attendees, bribery, illegal transfers, and foreign espionage are already in motion.  Factions: (1) Integrity Bloc – career officials, inspectors, or watchdog politicians who must expose the conspiracy and keep state secrets safe; (2) Conspiracy Bloc – crooked procurement officers, defense-industry lobbyists, and embedded foreign agents who want the transfer to go through and the paper trail erased.  Core Loop: Each day consists of (a) Plenary Debate – open discussion where new “Leak/Event” cards are revealed (e.g., ‘Redacted Contract Page Found’, ‘Overnight Database Crash’); (b) Accusation Vote – players nominate someone for dismissal or arrest; (c) Night Ops – Conspiracy Bloc secretly chooses one illegal action (bribe, data wipe, scapegoat, etc.), while special Integrity roles investigate.  Roles & Abilities: • Internal Inspector (peek at one player’s night action log without revealing how you obtained it) • Watchdog MP (may publicly subpoena one document, forcing a chosen player to reveal one secret card) • Corrupt Procurement Chief (can plant forged approval stamps, framing an innocent) • Arms Lobbyist (can spend ‘Funds’ tokens to buy silence, blocking one accusation) • Foreign Agent (once per game may extract a classified file, advancing Conspiracy victory track).  Legal Emphasis: Rules and flavor text reference Japan’s Three Principles on Arms Exports, the 2014 Transfer Guidelines, and the Act on the Protection of Specially Designated Secrets; revealing too much classified info in open debate triggers a penalty that can aid the Conspiracy Bloc.  Win Conditions: Integrity Bloc wins by eliminating all Conspiracy members or sabotaging the export license; Conspiracy Bloc wins if the export is approved OR if classified data is stolen. Debrief sheets link every in-game mechanic to real scandals such as the Lockheed bribery affair and recent JMOD bid-rigging cases, turning post-game reflection into a mini-seminar on defense-sector compliance.
